$$g\geq6r-(5r+s)=r-s.$$

$$g\leq\left\lfloor\frac{10r+2s}{10}\right\rfloor.$$

$$\frac{r-s}{10r+2s}
\leq\frac gn
\leq\frac1{10}.$$

$$\boxed{\frac gn\longrightarrow\frac1{10}.}$$

Theorem 3: unique ten-vertex positive equality graphACCEPT, subject to making the symmetry argument explicit in the final written proof.3.1 Equality ledgerSuppose
$$SF_2(G)-\beta_2(G)=1,\qquad n=10.$$
Using a maximizing minimal forming set  $S$ , equality holds throughout the universal gap proof.In particular,
$$a=p=0,\qquad u=2b,\qquad n=5b.$$
Thus
$$b=2.$$
Also,
$$|R|=2,\qquad |S|=6,\qquad |V(G)\setminus S|=4.$$
The equality in the incidence count forces every touched isolate to have exactly two chosen pair witnesses: there are two isolates, each with at least two incidences, and exactly four pair witnesses, each supplying at most one.Since there are no unused outside vertices, all four outside vertices are pair witnesses.Each pair witness has exactly its owner and one isolate as selected neighbours. Each of the four non-isolate selected vertices has exactly one such witness.These are the precise structural conclusions needed for the classification.3.2 Bipartition sizesLet  $b_A,b_B$  denote the numbers of selected isolates in the two bipartition classes.The equality structure gives side sizes
$$3b_A+2b_B,\qquad 2b_A+3b_B.$$
Each side is independent, so each has size at most
$$\beta_2(G)=5.$$
Since  $b_A+b_B=2$ , neither isolate pair can lie on the same side: that would give one side six vertices.Consequently,
$$b_A=b_B=1.$$
There are two supports and two witnesses on each side.3.3 No other possible edge typesThe equality structure fixes the following edges:each isolate has its two witness neighbours;each witness has its owner support neighbour and its isolate neighbour.There can be no edge between the two selected isolates, because they are already isolated in  $G[S]$ .There can be no additional support-to-witness edge, because each outside witness has exactly two selected neighbours.Therefore the only remaining possible edges are:
$$C_A-C_B,\qquad W_A-W_B.$$
Each of these is a bipartite graph with two vertices on either side.Hence  $G$  is a spanning subgraph of  $H$ , with possible deletions only among the four support edges and four witness edges.This reduction is correct.3.4 The symmetry argumentThe note asserts that all four support edges belong to one symmetry orbit, and all four witness edges belong to another.This is valid provided the relabelling includes the corresponding owner-witness permutations.The relevant transformations are:swap the two supports in one bipartition class;simultaneously swap the opposite-side witnesses whose owner is the corresponding support;independently perform the analogous operation in the other bipartition class.The witness graph is complete bipartite, so these simultaneous permutations preserve its internal edges.These transformations act transitively on the four support edges. They also act transitively on the four witness edges.I recommend explicitly writing these permutations in the proof rather than merely saying that the edges are equivalent. This is an exposition improvement, not a failure of the classification.3.5 Edge-deletion certificatesThe two supplied certificates are effective.For a missing support edge  $a_1b_1$ , use
$$D_C=\{a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,b_1,b_3\}.$$
After deleting that edge, the induced edges in this set are precisely
$$a_2b_1,\qquad a_4b_3.$$
Thus its induced maximum degree is one.For a missing witness edge  $a_4b_4$ , use
$$D_W=\{a_1,a_3,a_4,b_1,b_3,b_4\}.$$
Its induced edges are precisely
$$a_1b_1,\qquad a_3b_4,\qquad a_4b_3.$$
These are disjoint edges.In both cases the six-set is a dissociation set. Further edge deletions cannot invalidate it, because deleting edges cannot increase induced degrees.Therefore any missing one of the eight possible edges forces
$$\beta_2(G)\geq6,$$
contradicting  $\beta_2(G)=5$ .It follows that every one of the eight edges must be present, and hence
$$G\cong H.$$
The converse follows from the established parameters of  $H$ .The uniqueness proof is therefore sound.4. Final assessment and remaining boundariesThe important logical distinctions in the note are preserved:Theorem 1 is a genuine refinement of the universal bound. Its two inequalities use different degree hypotheses correctly.Theorem 2 proves asymptotic sharpness under minimum degree and two-connectivity, without claiming exact equality.Theorem 3 establishes uniqueness at the smallest positive equality order, not a classification of all equality graphs.The equality ledger also correctly implies that every positive unrounded equality graph has at least  $n/5$  vertices of full degree two. Thus no such graph can have minimum degree three.Recommended textual improvementsI would make only these two changes before treating the note as a polished mathematical presentation:In Theorem 2, explicitly state that after deletion of a block vertex, the surviving block remains connected by the Hamilton cycle, and that at least one of its two isolate attachments survives.In Theorem 3, list the generating support/witness permutations and explicitly identify the owner pairing used in the two deletion certificates.Neither requires a change to the proposed theorem statements or their constants.Overall ACCEPTFinal conclusion: I find no mathematical counterexample or substantive proof gap in the three proposed results, conditional on the stated established structural properties and parameters of  $H$  and the composition construction. The exact slack accounting, unused-witness incidence budget, two-connectivity for  $s=1$ , and ten-vertex uniqueness argument all withstand the audit. This is an independent ordinary-mathematics assessment, not a claim of new Lean verification or repository acceptance.

ACCEPT. For every integer  $r\ge2$ , the construction gives a finite simple, two-connected bipartite graph with
$$|V(L_r)|=10r,\qquad \beta_2(L_r)=5r,\qquad SF_2(L_r)=6r,$$
and no degree-four vertex. The proof is uniform in  $r$ ; it does not require enumeration.The concluding exclusion is valid for the stated four-attachment composition rule that preserves the four nonattachment degree-four vertices of each  $H$  copy, with their degrees unchanged. That preservation property is the precise scope of the counterexample.There are a few implicit steps worth spelling out, especially in minimality, but none requires a substantive repair.1. Construction, bipartition, and vertex countsThe global bipartition is
$$\begin{aligned}
A&=\{a_{j,t}:1\le j\le r,\ t=0,1\}
   \cup\{i_j,x_{j,0},x_{j,1}:1\le j\le r\},\\
B&=\{b_{j,t}:1\le j\le r,\ t=0,1\}
   \cup\{k_j,y_{j,0},y_{j,1}:1\le j\le r\}.
\end{aligned}$$
Every listed edge crosses these parts. Both parts have  $2r+3r=5r$  vertices, and the construction introduces no loops or repeated edges.The selected set contains the  $4r$  support vertices and the  $2r$  vertices  $i_j,k_j$ , so
$$|S|=6r.$$
2. The forming set is inclusion minimalUsing the stipulated definition, a vertex  $v\notin S$  must lie in a  $K_{1,2}$  whose other two vertices belong to  $S$ .For each omitted  $y_{j,t}$ , the edges
$$a_{j,t}y_{j,t},\qquad i_jy_{j,t}$$
give a covering star centered at  $y_{j,t}$ . Likewise, each omitted  $x_{j,t}$  is covered by the star centered at  $x_{j,t}$ , with leaves  $b_{j,t}$  and  $k_j$ . Thus  $S$  is forming.For minimality, the important point is to exclude both possible roles of a witness in a covering star.Deleting an ownerLet  $T=S\setminus\{a_{j,t}\}$ . Then
$$N(y_{j,t})\cap T=\{i_j\}.$$
Consequently: $y_{j,t}$  cannot be the center of a covering star, since it has only one selected neighbour.If  $y_{j,t}$  were a leaf, the center would have to be  $i_j$ . But  $i_j$  has no neighbour in  $T$ , so there is no selected second leaf.Thus  $y_{j,t}$  is uncovered. This is exactly what your phrase “only its isolated neighbour” establishes; making the leaf-role argument explicit would improve the presentation.Deleting  $b_{j,t}$  is symmetric, with witness  $x_{j,t}$  and isolated selected neighbour  $k_j$ .Deleting  $i_j$  or  $k_j$ After deleting  $i_j$  from  $S$ , the newly omitted vertex  $i_j$  has no selected neighbour: its only neighbours are  $y_{j,0}$  and  $y_{j,1}$ , both outside  $S$ . It therefore cannot belong to any covering star. The argument for  $k_j$  is identical.Finally, checking all single-vertex deletions does prove inclusion minimality here. The forming property is upward closed: if  $T$  forms and  $T\subseteq T'$ , every vertex outside  $T'$  retains its covering star from  $T$ . Hence a proper forming subset of  $S$  would imply that some single-vertex deletion from  $S$  also forms, which has just been excluded.Therefore
$$SF_2(L_r)\ge6r.$$
3. The eight-vertex dissociation lemma is correctWrite the module’s bipartition as
$$U=\{i,x_0,x_1,a_0,a_1\},\qquad
W=\{k,y_0,y_1\}.$$
Its edges are those of the six-cycle, together with  $a_0y_0,a_1y_1$ . In particular,
$$\deg(k)=2,\qquad \deg(y_0)=\deg(y_1)=3.$$
Recall that a dissociation set induces maximum degree at most one. Since this property is hereditary under taking subsets, excluding a six-element dissociation set also excludes every larger one.A six-element set has exactly the three possible part-size distributions you list.Distribution  $(5,1)$ All five vertices of  $U$  are selected. The selected vertex of  $W$  therefore retains all its neighbours and has selected degree at least two. Impossible.Distribution  $(4,2)$ At least one of the two selected vertices of  $W$  is a  $y_t$ , because  $k$  is the only vertex of  $W$  that is not a  $y$ . That  $y_t$  has three distinct neighbours in  $U$ . Only one vertex of  $U$  is omitted, so at least two of those neighbours are selected. Impossible.Distribution  $(3,3)$ All of  $W$  is selected. Each of  $i,x_0,x_1$  has two neighbours in  $W$ , so none can be selected. Only the two pendant vertices  $a_0,a_1$  remain eligible in  $U$ , whereas three vertices from  $U$  are required. Impossible.The entire part  $U$  is independent and has size five. Hence the module’s dissociation number is exactly five.There is no missing distribution or exceptional configuration.4. The six-cycle bound is correctLet its vertices be  $v_0,\ldots,v_5$ , with indices taken modulo six. For every dissociation set  $D$ ,
$$|D\cap\{v_j,v_{j+1},v_{j+2}\}|\le2,$$
because selecting all three would give the middle vertex two selected neighbours.Summing over the six cyclic windows counts each selected vertex three times:
$$3|D|\le12.$$
Thus  $|D|\le4$ .For completeness, selecting  $v_0,v_1,v_3,v_4$  induces two disjoint edges and attains four. Your proof gives the upper bound explicitly; this one sentence supplies attainment for the stated exact local value. The global argument only needs the upper bound.5. All support-intersection cases are coveredLet  $C_A,C_B$  be the two support sides, and let  $D$  be any global dissociation set.Both support sides are metPut
$$s=|D\cap C_A|,\qquad t=|D\cap C_B|,$$
and suppose  $s,t>0$ . Completeness of the support graph implies that every selected support in  $C_A$  has at least  $t$  selected neighbours, and every selected support in  $C_B$  has at least  $s$ . Therefore
$$s=t=1.$$
The restriction of  $D$  to each six-cycle remains a dissociation set, so each contributes at most four. Consequently,
$$|D|\le2+4r\le5r,$$
where the last inequality is precisely  $r\ge2$ .This remains valid even though the two selected supports may impose additional restrictions on their attached cycles: additional restrictions can only reduce the maximum. The proof does not assume that all the separate upper bounds can be attained simultaneously.At  $r=2$ , the displayed estimate is exactly  $10=5r$ , so the smallest permitted parameter is covered.Only the A support side is metNo vertex of  $C_B$  belongs to  $D$ . In the induced graph obtained by deleting  $C_B$ , all support-core edges disappear. What remains is exactly a disjoint union of  $r$  eight-vertex modules: the  $j$ -th six-cycle together with its two pendant  $a$ -owners.There are no surviving edges between different modules. The local bound therefore gives
$$|D|\le5r.$$
Only the B support side is metThe same argument applies with the two sides exchanged, again giving  $|D|\le5r$ .No support is selectedThen  $D$  is contained in the disjoint union of the  $r$  six-cycles, giving
$$|D|\le4r.$$
These cases exhaust all possibilities. Thus  $\beta_2(L_r)\le5r$ . Either whole bipartition side is an independent, hence dissociation, set of size  $5r$ , proving
$$\boxed{\beta_2(L_r)=5r}.$$
Using the accepted universal theorem now gives
$$SF_2(L_r)
\le \beta_2(L_r)+\left\lfloor\frac{10r}{10}\right\rfloor
=5r+r=6r.$$
Together with the explicit minimal forming set,
$$\boxed{SF_2(L_r)=6r}.$$
In particular, this establishes the positive unrounded equality
$$SF_2(L_r)-\beta_2(L_r)=r=\frac{|V(L_r)|}{10}.$$

$$K_{2r,2r}-v\cong K_{2r-1,2r}
\quad\text{or}\quad K_{2r,2r-1}.$$
Now delete an arbitrary vertex  $v$  of  $L_r$ .If  $v$  lies on a six-cycle, that cycle becomes a connected five-vertex path. Its four attachment endpoints  $x_{j,0},x_{j,1},y_{j,0},y_{j,1}$  are distinct, so at most one attachment is lost. The surviving path therefore still has at least three attachments to the unchanged connected support graph. Every other cycle remains intact and attached.If  $v$  is a support, every six-cycle remains intact. The cycle owning  $v$  loses one attachment and retains three; all other cycles retain four. The remaining support graph is connected.Thus  $L_r-v$  is connected for every vertex  $v$ . Since  $L_r$  has at least three vertices, this proves two-connectivity.There is no hidden issue involving a disconnected remnant of a module: deleting one vertex from a cycle leaves a single path.7. The degree calculation is exactVertex typeNumber of verticesDegree $i_j,k_j$  $2r$  $2$  $x_{j,t},y_{j,t}$  $4r$  $3$  $a_{j,t},b_{j,t}$  $4r$  $2r+1$ Each support has  $2r$  neighbours in the support core and exactly one owner edge. $$m(D_j)\subseteq N_T(D_j)=F_j.$$

$$|m(D_j)|=|D_j|=|F_j|,$$
hence
$$m(D_j)=F_j.$$

$$\mathbf 1_{\{m(b)\in F_j\}}=\mathbf 1_{\{b\in D_j\}},
\qquad
\phi_T(m(b))=\phi_B(b).$$

$$\sum_{t\in T}\phi_T(t)=\sum_{b\in B}\phi_B(b),
\qquad

A_{\mathrm{tot}}-B_{\mathrm{tot}}
&=\sum_{t\in T}\bigl(\phi_T(t)-\phi_B(\pi(t))\bigr)\\

Exact definitions and the elementary coverage criterionFor a graph  $F$ , a selected set  $T\subseteq V(F)$ , and any vertex  $z$ , write
$$N_T^F(z)=N_F(z)\cap T.$$
When the graph is clear, omit the superscript.A vertex  $x\notin T$  is covered when there are two distinct vertices of  $T$  which, together with  $x$ , contain a not necessarily induced  $K_{1,2}$ . Thus
$$x\text{ is covered by }T
\iff
|N_T(x)|\ge 2
\quad\text{or}\quad
\exists y\in N_T(x):N_T(y)\ne\varnothing.
\tag{1}$$
Indeed, the first alternative makes  $x$  the centre. In the second, choose  $z\in N_T(y)$ ; the edges  $xy,yz$  give a star centred at  $y$ . The three vertices are distinct because  $x\notin T$ ,  $y,z\in T$ , and the graph is simple. Conversely, these are the two possible roles of  $x$  in a witnessing star.Consequently,
$$x\text{ is uncovered by }T
\iff
N_T(x)=\varnothing
\quad\text{or}\quad
\bigl[N_T(x)=\{y\}\ \text{and}\ N_T(y)=\varnothing\bigr].
\tag{2}$$
The singleton alternative includes an existential quantifier over  $y$ .This criterion is valid in graphs containing triangles: an additional edge between the leaves is harmless. For induced stars, criterion (1) would require additional nonadjacency conditions.The parameters should be defined explicitly:
$$\operatorname{SF}_2(F)
=
\max\{|T|:T\text{ is an inclusion-minimal forming set of }F\},$$
and
$$\beta_2(F)
=
\max\{|D|:\text{every vertex of }F[D]\text{ has degree at most }1\}.$$

If  $T$  forms  $F$  and  $T\subseteq U$ , then  $U$  forms  $F$ .Every vertex outside  $U$  was outside  $T$ , and its old witness remains available. Therefore a forming set is inclusion-minimal if and only if every single-vertex deletion fails. This justifies the minimality conclusion from the protected witnesses.2. $$T=S\setminus\{v\},\qquad D=C\setminus\{v\}.$$

$$x\in V(G)\setminus\bigl(V(B)\cup T\bigr).$$

$$xp,\quad pv.$$

$$y\in C\setminus\{v\},\qquad py\in E(B).$$

$$x\in V(B)\setminus(C\cup P).$$
Because  $x\notin P$ , it has no external neighbours, so
$$N_S^G(x)=N_C^B(x).$$
If this set has at least two vertices, the first alternative of (A) holds. Then  $S=\{p,z\}$  forms the extended graph through  $x-p-z$ , although  $C$  does not form  $B$ .Accordingly, retain the cap predicate’s quantification over all  $C$  satisfying (A). Exact composition: make the construction explicitReplace the opening of the composition section by the following hypothesis:Let  $B_1,\dots,B_m$  be finitely many finite simple graphs with pairwise disjoint vertex sets, and let  $P_i\subseteq V(B_i)$ . Let  $G$  have vertex set
$$V(G)=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^m V(B_i)$$
and edge set
$$E(G)=\bigcup_{i=1}^m E(B_i)\ \cup F,$$
where every edge of  $F$  joins a vertex of  $P_i$  to a vertex of  $P_j$  for distinct  $i,j$ .This ensures that the blocks exhaust  $G$ , remain induced, and have actual boundaries contained in their prescribed  $P_i$ .Assume the stated caps and protected-witness hypotheses. Put
$$S=\bigcup_{i=1}^m C_i.$$
Formation survivesEvery  $x\notin S$  lies in a unique block  $B_i$ , and its internal witness under  $C_i$  remains a witness under  $S$ . Thus  $S$  forms  $G$ .Every deletion failsFix  $v\in C_i$ , and set
$$T=S\setminus\{v\},\qquad D=C_i\setminus\{v\}.$$

$$x\in V(B_i)\setminus P_i,\qquad x\notin D.$$
Disjointness gives  $x\notin T$ . Since  $x$  has no external edges,
$$N_T^G(x)=N_D^{B_i}(x).
\tag{3}$$
If the right-hand side is empty,  $x$  is uncovered by (2).Otherwise it is  $\{y\}$ , where  $y\notin P_i$  and
$$N_D^{B_i}(y)=\varnothing.$$
The nonboundary condition on  $y$  gives
$$N_T^G(y)=N_D^{B_i}(y)=\varnothing.
\tag{4}$$

$$|S|=\sum_i |C_i|=\sum_i s_i,$$
and hence
$$\operatorname{SF}_2(G)\ge\sum_i s_i.$$
The caps give the matching upper boundFor any inclusion-minimal forming set  $T$  of  $G$ , the cap theorem applies separately to every induced block:
$$|T\cap V(B_i)|\le s_i.$$
Because the blocks partition  $V(G)$ ,
$$|T|=\sum_i|T\cap V(B_i)|\le\sum_i s_i.$$
Therefore
$$\boxed{\operatorname{SF}_2(G)=\sum_i s_i.}$$
No bipartiteness is used anywhere in this proof.Calling each  $C_i$  internally minimal is harmless but redundant: internal formation and the protected failure condition already imply internal minimality.4. The dissociation formula and the precise role of bipartitenessWrite the prescribed bipartitions as
$$V(B_i)=L_i\sqcup R_i,\qquad |L_i|=|R_i|=b_i,$$
and suppose
$$\beta_2(B_i)=b_i.$$
For every dissociation set  $D$  in  $G$ , its restriction to each block is a dissociation set there. Consequently,
$$|D|
=\sum_i|D\cap V(B_i)|
\le\sum_i\beta_2(B_i)
=\sum_i b_i.
\tag{5}$$
This upper bound does not require bipartiteness.Under the stated side-respecting hypothesis,
$$L=\bigcup_iL_i$$
is independent and has cardinality  $\sum_i b_i$ . It is therefore a dissociation set, proving
$$\boxed{\beta_2(G)=\sum_i b_i.}$$
“Respect these chosen sides” should explicitly mean that every added edge joins
$$\bigcup_i L_i\quad\text{to}\quad\bigcup_i R_i.$$
There is a useful precision improvement: global bipartiteness alone suffices, even without compatibility with the originally named sides. Indeed,
$$|V(G)|=2\sum_i b_i.$$
If  $G$  is bipartite, a larger global bipartition class is independent and has size at least  $|V(G)|/2=\sum_i b_i$ . Combined with (5), this proves equality.Thus an optional weaker statement is:If  $G$  is bipartite—in particular, if all added edges respect the prescribed block sides—then (C) holds.Separate bipartiteness of the blocks is insufficient. For example, take two disjoint  $C_4$ ’s and add every edge between them. Each block has balanced parts of size  $2$  and dissociation number  $2$ , but the resulting graph has dissociation number  $2$ , not  $4$ . Any three vertices within one block contain a degree-two vertex; any three vertices meeting both blocks have a vertex adjacent to the other two.Your absence of connectivity or port-degree restrictions is otherwise correct. Even for (C), the graph on block indices need not be bipartite; the relevant bipartition is on the actual vertices of  $G$ .5. The proposed five-vertex counterexample is correctThe ambient graph is the path
$$x-p-v-a-b,$$
with
$$B=G[\{p,v,a,b\}],\qquad P=\{p\},\qquad
S=C=\{p,v,a,b\}.$$
Initially, the only outside vertex is  $x$ , covered by  $x-p-v$ .After deleting  $v$ , the selected set inside  $B$  is
$$D=\{p,a,b\}.$$
The only vertex of  $B$  outside  $D$  is  $v$ , which has two selected neighbours  $p,a$ . Thus  $D$  forms  $B$ .Globally, however,
$$N_D(x)=\{p\},\qquad N_D(p)=\varnothing,$$
so  $x$  is uncovered. Condition (2) of the deletion lemma fails precisely at  $p$ : its unique selected internal neighbour was  $v$ .This example already lies in the bipartite class. It refutes deletion based on internal formation alone even there. The safe-deletion lemma does not require  $S$  to be minimal, so the absence of that property in the example causes no difficulty.What “necessary safeguard” meansThe example proves that the boundary-activity hypothesis cannot simply be dropped from a general safe-deletion theorem. It does not make that hypothesis necessary for every deletion in a fixed ambient graph, where other selected vertices may supply replacement activity.There is, however, a stronger exact statement:Given hypothesis (1), condition (2) is necessary and sufficient for deletion safety uniformly over all permitted ambient extensions and forming sets with intersection  $C$ .Sufficiency is the lemma. For necessity, suppose condition (2) fails at  $p$ . Then
$$N_C^B(p)=\{v\}.$$

The new vertex  $x$  is covered by  $x-p-v$ , so  $S$  forms the extension. After deletion,  $x$  has sole selected neighbour  $p$ , and  $p$  has no selected neighbour. $$1-2-3-4,$$
and choose
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}

B_1&\{1,2,3\}&\{3\}&\{1,3\}\\
B_2&\{2,3,4\}&\{2\}&\{2,4\}
\end{array}
\qquad s_1=s_2=2.$$

Deleting  $u$  preserves internal formation and the port’s selected neighbour  $w$ , establishing the cap predicate.The set  $\{u,p\}$  forms the block.Deleting  $u$  has protected witness  $x=u$ , with no selected neighbour.Deleting  $p$  has protected witness  $x=w$ , whose unique selected neighbour  $u$  is interior and has no selected neighbour.Nevertheless,
$$C_1\cup C_2=V(G)$$
is not minimal:  $\{2,3\}$  already forms  $G$ . In fact,
$$\operatorname{SF}_2(P_4)=3<4=s_1+s_2.$$
